items.title: Impairments Five and Six: Aspiring to the Wrong Reward, and Neglecting Protocol

items.zh: 又自執取睡眠為樂、偃臥為樂、脇臥為樂；性不翹勤；為性懶惰；不具起發；於諸有智同梵行者，不能時時覲問供事。是名放逸懈怠所攝。云何名為發起邪願？謂如有一，依止邪願修行梵行。言我所有若戒、若禁，若常精勤、若修梵行，當得生天，或餘天處。或復愛樂利養恭敬，而修梵行。謂因此故，從他希求利養恭敬；即於如是利養恭敬，深生染著。如是名為發起邪願。云何軌則虧損所攝？謂如有一，於威儀路、或所作事、或諸善品加行處所所有軌則，不順世間，違越世間；不順毘奈耶，違越毘奈耶。如前廣說。
items.en: Further, such a person clings to sleep as pleasurable, to lying supine as pleasurable, to lying on the side as pleasurable; is by nature reluctant, by nature lazy, never fully rousing effort; and is unable, from time to time, to visit, consult, and serve wise fellow practitioners. This is called being subsumed under heedlessness and laziness. What is called giving rise to a misguided aspiration? It is like one who cultivates pure conduct resting on a misguided aspiration, saying: "Through all my discipline and restraint, through constant diligence, through cultivating pure conduct, may I be reborn in a heaven, or some other heavenly realm." Or one who cultivates pure conduct out of delight in support and veneration. …This is called giving rise to a misguided aspiration. What is called being subsumed under impairment of protocol? It is like one whose protocol, in the pathways of deportment, in the tasks performed, or in the settings for wholesome endeavour, does not conform to worldly convention and violates it, does not conform to the Vinaya and violates it — to be understood at length as stated before.

items.zh: 是名軌則虧損所攝。云何淨命虧損所攝？

items.title: Impairment Seven: Wrong Livelihood, and the Art of Faking Sanctity for Alms

items.zh: 謂如有一，為性大欲，不知喜足，難養難滿。常以非法追求衣服、飲食、臥具、病緣醫藥及諸資具，不以正法。又為貪求種種衣服、飲食、臥具、病緣醫藥資具因緣，方便顯己有勝功德，矯詐構集非常威儀。為誑他故，恒常詐現諸根無掉、諸根無動、諸根寂靜，由是令他謂其有德，當有所施、當有所作。所謂承事，供給衣服、飲食、臥具、病緣醫藥及諸資具。又多凶悖、強口、矯傲、修飾其名、執恃種姓。或求多聞，或住持法，為利養故，亦復為他宣說正法。或佛所說，或弟子說，或自宣說己實有德，或少增益。或於他前方便現相，為求衣服，或求隨一沙門資具。或為求多，或求精妙，雖無匱乏，而現被服故弊衣裳，為令淨信長者、居士、婆羅門等、知其衣服有所匱乏，殷重承事，給施眾多上妙衣服。
items.en: It is like one who is, by nature, of great desire, never knowing contentment, hard to nourish, hard to satisfy — constantly seeking robes, food, bedding, medicine for illness, and other requisites through improper means, not through proper means. …Further, for the sake of robes, food, bedding, medicine, and other requisites, one contrives, by skilful means, to display an appearance of excellent virtue, fraudulently assembling an unusual deportment. To deceive others, one constantly, falsely displays faculties free of agitation, free of movement, utterly still — leading others to believe one possesses genuine virtue and ought to be given offerings and service. …Further, one is often fierce, obstinate, forcing one's words, arrogant, embellishing one's reputation, relying on claims of noble lineage. …One seeks extensive learning, or retains the Dharma in memory, for the sake of material gain, and, on that basis, teaches the true Dharma to others. …Or, in front of others, one contrives to display a certain appearance in order to obtain robes, or some other monastic requisite. …Though not actually lacking, one displays worn, tattered robes, so that faithful elders, householders, and brahmins, believing one's robes to be genuinely lacking, will earnestly attend and provide an abundance of fine, excellent robes.

items.zh: 如為衣服，為餘隨一沙門資生眾具亦爾。

items.title: Section: The Ten Impairments Complete — Two Extremes, False Austerity, and Outright Degradation

items.zh: 或於淨信長者、居士、婆羅門所，如其所欲不得稱遂，或彼財物有所闕乏，求不得時，即便強逼、研磨麁語，而苦求索。或彼財物無所闕乏，得下劣時，便對施主現前毀棄所得財物。如是告言：咄哉男子！某善男子、某善女人，方汝族姓及以財寶，極為下劣，又極貧匱，而能惠施如是如是多妙悅意資產眾具；汝望於彼，族姓尊貴，財寶豐饒，何為但施如是少劣非悅意物？彼由如是或依矯詐、或邪妄語、或假現相、或苦研逼、或利求利種種狀相，而從他所非法希求所有衣服、飲食、臥具、病緣醫藥諸資生具，非以正法而有所求。由非法故，說名邪命。如是名為尸羅淨命虧損所攝。云何名為墮在二邊？謂如有一，耽著受用極樂行邊，從他所得或法非法所有衣服、飲食、臥具、病緣醫藥及諸資具，愛玩受用，不觀過患、不知出離。是名一邊。復有一類，好求受用自苦行邊，以無量門而自煎迫，受極苦楚。謂依棘刺、或依灰坌、或依木杵、或依木板、或狐蹲住、或狐蹲坐修斷瑜伽。或復事火，謂乃至三承事於火。或復昇水，謂乃至三昇上其水。或一足住，隨日而轉。或復所餘。如是等類修自苦行，是第二邊。如是名為墮在二邊。云何名為不能出離？謂如有一，或戒或禁由見執取。謂我因此若戒若禁，當得清淨、解脫、出離。一切外道所有禁戒，雖善防護、雖善清淨，如其清淨，不名出離。如是名為不能出離。云何名為所受失壞？謂如有一，都無羞恥，不顧沙門，毀犯淨戒，習諸惡法。內懷腐敗，外現貞實，猶如淨水所生蝸牛、螺音狗行。實非沙門，自稱沙門；實非梵行，自稱梵行。如是名為所受失壞。略由如是十種因緣，名戒虧損。世尊或說尸羅虧損，或時復說尸羅艱難。當知於彼諸因緣中，由二因緣，謂不能出離，及所受失壞。由餘因緣，當知唯說尸羅虧損。
items.en: Or, before a faithful elder, householder, or brahmin, when what one desires is not granted … one then forcibly presses and grinds down with harsh speech, bitterly demanding it. …Or, when one's wealth is in no way lacking, upon receiving something inferior, one openly disparages the gift before the donor … "why give only something so paltry and displeasing?" …It is like one who indulges in the extreme of pleasure … perceiving no fault, knowing no renunciation. This is one extreme. There is, further, a kind that delights in seeking the extreme of self-affliction, tormenting oneself through countless methods, enduring extreme suffering — standing on thorns, covering oneself in ashes, standing on a wooden post or plank, crouching like a fox, worshipping fire three times daily, rising up out of the water three times [by climbing posts], standing on one leg and turning to follow the sun. …This is called falling into the two extremes. …It is like one who, through a mistaken view, clings to some discipline or vow, saying: "Through this discipline, this vow, I shall attain purity, liberation, deliverance." …Whatever discipline non-Buddhist practitioners hold, however well-guarded, however outwardly pure, purity of that kind is not called deliverance. This is called being unable to attain liberation. …It is like one who, entirely without shame, giving no thought to being a renunciant, violates the pure precepts and habitually practices evil things. …Inwardly rotten, outwardly appearing genuine — like a filthy snail formed in clean water — a voice like a conch, conduct like a dog: not truly a renunciant, yet calling oneself one; not truly practising pure conduct, yet calling it so. This is called letting what was received degrade. In brief, through these ten causes and conditions, discipline is said to be impaired.

blocks.text: The rest of the ten impairments. The description of wrong livelihood is vivid: a catalogue of ways a renunciant can fake holiness for gain.

Laziness "clings to sleep, lying supine and on the side as pleasurable", and fails to attend on wise companions. Venerable Miào Jìng: one should visit them regularly and ask, "How should I practise?" **Wrong aspiration**: "Through all my discipline may I be reborn in a heaven." Master Cháng Bǎi: that place is still within saṃsāra.

"By nature of great desire, never content, hard to nourish": constantly seeking requisites by improper means. Venerable Miào Jìng: wanting more than one has is "great desire"; having enough and not being satisfied is "never content". The methods: displaying an appearance of virtue; flattering speech; hinting; pressing donors with harsh words; belittling small gifts; using one gift to get another. Master Cháng Bǎi notes why robes are the example: in ancient times cloth was precious.

"One indulges in the extreme of pleasure…; another delights in the extreme of self-affliction." Master Cháng Bǎi: keeping precepts should follow the middle way too. Venerable Miào Jìng's image for the middle path: two posts in the water, one gripped by the hand, one under the foot, and one climbs out.

subs.head: Unable to reach liberation; degraded discipline

blocks.text: Clinging to a discipline with wrong view ("through this I shall attain purity") cannot liberate. And one who has received the precepts but is "inwardly rotten, outwardly genuine" lets them degrade completely. Master Cháng Bǎi: the first eight are "impairment"; this last is ruin.

quiz.q: What does the treatise describe as "subsumed under heedlessness and laziness"?
options: clinging to sleep and lying down as pleasure; reluctant, lazy, never rousing effort; not attending on wise fellow practitioners
quiz.why: "Clings to sleep, lying supine, and lying on the side as pleasurable; is reluctant, lazy, never fully rousing effort; and is unable to attend on wise fellow practitioners from time to time." Venerable Miào Jìng: heedlessness is following afflictions; laziness is different.

quiz.q: What does the treatise call "giving rise to a misguided aspiration"?
options: practising pure conduct for heavenly rebirth, or out of love for support and veneration
quiz.why: "Saying: through all my discipline and restraint, diligence, and pure conduct, may I be reborn in a heaven. Or one who cultivates pure conduct out of delight in support and veneration." Venerable Miào Jìng: misguided aspirations are of the future (heaven) and the present (gain).

quiz.q: Why is wishing for heavenly rebirth a misguided aspiration, per Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: the place one wishes for is still within saṃsāra; afflictions are not severed
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: because the place one wishes to be born is still within the cycle of birth and death; afflictions are not severed. Such a wrong aspiration is already bound up with greed, unnoticed.

quiz.q: How do the masters distinguish "great desire" from "never content"?
options: wanting more of what one lacks is great desire; not satisfied with what one has is discontent
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: not having something yet wanting more is "great desire"; having it yet not being satisfied is "never content." Master Cháng Bǎi: wanting what one lacks and, having it, wanting more — that is a nature of great desire.

quiz.q: How does the treatise describe "faking a sanctified deportment"?
options: to obtain requisites, contriving an unusual deportment, constantly feigning stilled faculties so others think one virtuous and give
quiz.why: "One contrives to display an appearance of excellent virtue, fraudulently assembling an unusual deportment. To deceive others, one constantly falsely displays faculties free of agitation, still — leading others to believe one has virtue." Venerable Miào Jìng: inwardly great desire, outwardly an appearance of desirelessness.

quiz.q: What are the "two extremes" the treatise describes?
options: indulging in extreme pleasure; seeking extreme self-affliction — thorns, ashes, posts, crouching, fire worship, water, standing on one leg turning with the sun
quiz.why: "One indulges in the extreme of pleasure… This is one extreme. There is, further, a kind that delights in the extreme of self-affliction, tormenting oneself through countless methods." Master Cháng Bǎi: austerity is mistaken — practice is a transformation of the mind, not bodily suffering.

quiz.q: The ascetic practice "升水" is rendered "immersing oneself in water three times." How does Venerable Miào Jìng explain it?
options: citing Dunlun: two posts in the water; holding one and stepping on the other, one rises up out of the water
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: there are two posts set in the water; holding one with a hand and stepping on the other with a foot, one rises up out of the water. The English "immersing" differs.
